Caption: Fig. 1.6. Variation of the turbine entry temperature (TET) during a typical flight cycle of a civil
aircraft.
Title: Variation of the turbine entry temperature (TET) during a typical flight cycle
Trend: The plot shows the Turbine Entry Temperature (TET) profile over a 108-minute flight. TET begins at 'Ground idle', spikes to its maximum during 'Take-off' (0-2 min), remains high during 'Climb' (2-23 min), then drops to a sustained level for 'Cruise' (23-86 min). It decreases further for 'Approach' and 'Flight idle' (86-107 min), has a brief spike for 'Reverse thrust' upon landing, and returns to 'Ground idle'. This illustrates the highly variable thermal loading on engine components during a single flight.

Caption: Fig. 1.14. Performance diagram illustrating the variation of the specific fuel consumption (defined
as normalised fuel burn/thrust developed) against thrust, for various values of the TET and OPR.
Title: Performance diagram: Specific fuel consumption vs. Thrust
Trend: This performance map plots specific fuel consumption against thrust. It features two sets of contour lines: one for constant Turbine Entry Temperature (TET) and another for constant Overall Pressure Ratio (OPR). The general trend shows that for a given thrust, specific fuel consumption decreases with increasing TET. Similarly, at a constant TET, increasing the OPR generally improves fuel efficiency (lowers SFC). Optimal performance is found at high TET and high OPR.

Caption: Fig. 1.16. Values of the Larson–Miller parameter, P, for a number of high-temperature materials.
The horizontal and near-vertical lines have spacings equivalent to a factor of 2 change in creep life
and 200°C temperature capability, respectively; the materials which display the best
high-temperature performance lie towards the top right of the diagram. Adapted from a graph
provided by Dan Miracle.
Title: Larson-Miller Parameter for High-Temperature Materials
Trend: This Larson-Miller plot compares the creep resistance of various high-temperature materials by plotting applied stress against the Larson-Miller parameter. Materials positioned towards the top-right exhibit superior high-temperature performance. Refractory alloys like Mo-41Re and ThO2-W, and advanced single-crystal superalloys like RR3000, CMSX-4, and SRR99, show the highest creep strength. Polycrystalline superalloys (Waspaloy), titanium alloys (Ti-6242), and various intermetallics occupy lower performance regimes on the chart.

Caption: Fig. 1.17. Evolution of the high-temperature capability of the superalloys over a 60 year period
since their emergence in the 1940s.
Title: Evolution of the high-temperature capability of the superalloys
Trend: The chart illustrates a significant and steady improvement in the high-temperature creep capability of superalloys from 1940 to 2010. The temperature at which alloys can survive for 1000 hours under 137 MPa stress has increased from around 750°C to over 1100°C. This progress is marked by a clear evolution in processing technology, moving from wrought alloys to conventionally cast, then to directionally solidified, and finally to single-crystal alloys, each step enabling higher temperature performance. Specific alloy developments are marked along the trend line.

Caption: Fig. 3.29. Variation of the creep rupture lives of the single-crystal superalloys TMS-75 and TMS-82+, as a function of the amount of y' phase [27]. The creep rupture life is largest when the y' fraction is about 70%. (Courtesy of Hiroshi Harada.)
Title: Variation of the creep rupture lives of single-crystal superalloys
Trend: The chart shows creep rupture life on a logarithmic scale versus the volume fraction of the γ' phase for two alloys (TMS-75 and TMS-82+) at two temperatures (900 °C and 1100 °C). For all four conditions, the creep rupture life exhibits a distinct peak at approximately 70% γ' volume fraction.
